confidence_note: Book text not read. The Hadza 100-150 g figure is the book's estimate (p.17), not a measurement; Americans' 15 g is Sonnenburg's 2017 Stanford quote. The seasonal Hadza study (2017) and the low-fiber mouse study (2016) are later work of the Sonnenburg lab, not in the 2015 book. Old claims on butyrate, disease rates and 'twice the diversity' omitted.
facts: The Hadza are a population of just over 1,000 in Tanzania's Rift Valley, fewer than 200 following the traditional life; diet of meat, berries, baobab, tubers and honey.
The book says the Hadza eat 100 to 150 grams of fiber a day; this is an estimate, not a measurement.
Justin Sonnenburg (2017): 'We average 15 grams per day', speaking of the industrialized world.
The book cites a comparison in which US adults had the least diverse gut microbiota next to two nonindustrial populations in South America and Africa.
The book cites a study of 76 to 95-year-olds in which more dietary fiber went with more short-chain fatty acids.
One summary says that when fiber is scarce, gut bacteria feed on the mucus lining and weaken the gut barrier.

Later Sonnenburg-lab study: 350 stool samples from 188 Hadza over about a year; some species fell in the wet season (honey-heavy) and returned in the dry season (tuber-heavy); samples from the same season a year apart were nearly identical.

Sonnenburg-lab mouse study: moving mice from high-fiber to low-fiber diet reduced about 60 percent of bacterial species in number; after four generations of low-fiber feeding some species did not return; whether this harms health is not established.
scene_details: tubers eaten in the dry season
mice moved to a low-fiber diet
tension: The Hadza eat several times the fiber of an industrialized diet, and their gut community follows the seasons, while in mice a low-fiber diet can cost species for good.
opening_idea: The Hadza live on tubers and baobab, and a Stanford microbiologist set their gut against ours.

lessons.idea: Feed the gut a variety of fibers, not the same few meals.
lessons.anchor: the Hadza's seasonal tubers and the species lost in low-fiber mice

reflect_final: Which fiber-rich food that you rarely buy could you add to this week's shopping list?

pocket_idea: Hadza hunter-gatherers get over 100 grams of fiber a day; add one rarely eaten plant to this week's meals.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: The Hadza get 100 grams of fiber a day or more, against about 15 in the industrialized diet.
